transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-17
Start time: 16:30 PT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Derek Owens (Redwood SE), Liam Patel (AtlasForge Head of ML), Sofia Romero (Platform Eng), Oliver Wang (CTO)

Summary:
Quick discovery for AtlasForge's intent to exit their current vendor (they mentioned OpenAI + vLLM internal serving) and evaluate Redwood's hosted vs dedicated vs private options. Focus areas: compatibility with TGI/vLLM workflows, eval parity, latency/cost tradeoff, data residency and KMS integration.

Topics:
- Current stack and pain points
- Migration blockers and success criteria
- Benchmark/eval plan and pilot
- Security/compliance requirements
- Next steps

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick intros, i'm Maya from Redwood, AE; with me is Derek, our systems engineer. how are you all?
[00:06] Liam: hey, Liam here, head of ML at AtlasForge. we have Sofia (platform) and Oliver (cto) on. thanks for the time.
[00:14] Derek: great to meet you. quick high-level, we're expecting this call to be... sort of discovery + scoping, we want to understand your current infra and blockers if you were to move off your existing provider.
[00:23] Sofia: yup, we're planning a vendor exit, mostly because cost exploded and we can't get consistent latency with small tail queries. we also have more on-prem needs for certain clients.
[00:33] Oliver: and we need to avoid vendor lock; we currently run a hybrid: some calls go to OpenAI hosted, some to our vllm cluster for batch; we've been testing TGI adapters as well.
[00:43] Maya: good, that's exactly the pattern we see. can you walk us through the current flow and what 'eval parity' means for you?
[00:49] Liam: sure, so production path is: API -> request router -> if it's low latency small prompt we hit OpenAI; if >2k tokens or for heavy workloads we send to v-L-M cluster, that's our internal service. for some models we use T-G-I fine tuned variants. parity means same quality/latency/cost metrics for our regression prompt set — and we need exact match type of outputs for key flows.
[01:12] Derek: when you say 'exact match' are you flexible on small tokenization differences? sometimes embedding or tokenizers differ.
[01:19] Liam: we get that. key is that user-visible behaviors (summaries, completions) need to be within our threshold. we have a prompt-set of ~500 test cases.
[01:29] Sofia: and importantly, we can't send sensitive customer data to a third-party hosted endpoint for certain clients — so VPC/private is on the table.
[01:37] Maya: makes sense. can you do a quick list of top pain points? we want to be sure we map features.
[01:42] Oliver: cost unpredictability, cold-start latencies when our worker pool scales down, KV cache miss behavior between vllm nodes, and the lack of standardized rollout tooling.
[01:54] Maya: note — Redwood has dedicated capacity + prefix/KV caching and rollout features. Derek, maybe you explain options: hosted, dedicated, private.
[02:02] Derek: sure. hosted is our SaaS API, fastest to get started, pay per token, with option to pin model versions. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools that you control via policies and get predictable throughput. Private is a VPC or on-prem control plane where you manage the network, KMS, and we provide the runtime package. For sensitive data we often recommend private with HSM/KMS integrations.
[02:24] Liam: for dedicated, do you isolate workloads? we need tenancy separation for clients.
[02:29] Derek: yes, dedicated gives isolated pools per customer; we also support RBAC and network ACLs. you can run multiple pools with different quantization profiles.
[02:37] Sofia: what about model compatibility? Our current finetuned TGI models — can those just run on Redwood, or do we need to rework weight formats?
[02:47] Derek: compatibility depends on format. we support most HF weights, GGUF, and common TGI artifacts but sometimes tokenizers or custom ops need minor changes. we've migrated customers from TGI with a short conversion step. we also support vLLM-like runtimes via our adapter layer, but i want to flag: quantization and certain custom operators for TGI might need a preflight test.
[03:11] Liam: ok, so we'd need an eval run. latency: currently 90th percentile for small requests is around 140ms in vLLM for warm workers, but OpenAI has a 60-80ms for the same prompts. cost per 1M tokens... you get the idea. can you give rough delta?
[03:29] Maya: we can — hosted usually trades a slight increase in avg latency vs optimized vllm on-prem, but we give you a lot of operations and caching that reduce token spend. dedicated tends to hit similar latency to your tuned vllm if we size correctly.
[03:42] Derek: also for tail-latency, continuous batching and fast KV cache are key — Redwood runtime has prefix caching that cuts repeated context costs a lot.
[03:50] Sofia: data residency — for EU customers, we need data never leaving region. can private do that?
[03:55] Derek: yes, private in a regional VPC or on-prem ensures no cross-region egress; we can integrate with your KMS and put logs into your SIEM.
[04:04] Oliver: SOC2 is required, and audit logs need to be retained for 13 months.
[04:09] Maya: we have SOC2 Type II and can provide audit artifacts; retention duration for logs is configurable in private/dedicated plans.
[04:17] Liam: excellent. a couple more tech blockers: we rely heavily on streaming tokens for chat — will Redwood's streaming match our behavior? also function/tool calling for our orchestration layer.
[04:26] Derek: streaming is supported, and function calling/structured outputs are supported; sometimes the webhooks or streaming latencies differ by client connection. for most customers it's identical.
[04:36] Maya: maybe we can propose a pilot: we'll run your 500-case prompt set across your hosted and your dedicated environment, compare outputs and perf. we'll do token-accuracy, latency, and cost per 1k tokens.
[04:47] Liam: that's the plan. ownership: who runs the first run? we prefer Redwood to run hosted + dedicated baseline and then we'll run vllm baseline.
[04:55] Derek: that's fine. we typically do a smoke run on hosted to get baseline, then spin a small dedicated pool sized for your QPS. we'll need model artifacts and tokenizer configs; if some ops fail we'll convert.
[05:08] Sofia: regarding conversion, timeline? we have a quarterly release window, so need to be in pilot in 2 weeks ideally.
[05:15] Maya: feasible. action plan: Maya will send options and pricing, Derek will attach security/SOC2/KMS docs, and Liam will confirm dataset. timing: we aim to start pilot by Feb 24.
[05:26] Oliver: budget question: how do you price dedicated? reserved commit vs burst?
[05:32] Derek: dedicated is usually a monthly commit for a GPU pool; we support burst credits for spiky traffic. we can model expected total cost delta vs your current infrastructure if you share usage metrics.
[05:44] Liam: we'll share token volumes and request distribution. we also need to know if we can bring existing vllm caches or if we need to retrain a caching strategy.
[05:53] Derek: you can't import live KV caches; we recommend seeding KV caches with popular prefixes and Redwood's runtime will warm caches using recent traffic logs.
[06:02] Sofia: any gotchas on SSO / SAML? our internal teams will want RBAC integration and SCIM.
[06:09] Maya: we do SSO via SAML/OIDC and support SCIM provisioning for user management in the console.
[06:16] Oliver: what about model rollouts — can we do canary and A/B testing with automatic fallback to previous models?
[06:22] Derek: yes, our rollout engine supports percentage-based canaries, A/B and automatic fallback based on error/latency thresholds.
[06:29] Liam: perfect. competition: we've talked to Anthropic and Azure OpenAI as well — any big differences we should be aware of?
[06:36] Maya: Anthropic and Azure are strong for model quality in some families; the big difference is control and cost predictability. Redwood focuses on serving economics and deployment flexibility.
[06:46] Sofia: ok, next - security review. we will need a dedicated review if we pursue private. could you outline typical integration points?
[06:54] Derek: sure: 1) network: VPC peering or private link; 2) keys: we integrate with KMS/HSM via customer-managed keys; 3) logs: forward to your SIEM via secure channel; 4) auth: SSO/SAML and service-to-service mTLS; 5) compliance artifacts: SOC2 reports, pen test results.
[07:13] Liam: are there references for customers with similar on-prem needs?
[07:17] Maya: yes, we'll share a short list (we can't share everything, but a couple of similar regulated customers we can reference).
[07:24] Oliver: about migration sequencing — we have 20+ models. do you recommend migrating a subset first?
[07:30] Derek: absolutely. recommended: pick 1-2 critical models as pilot, run eval parity tests, then expand. you can route only a percentage of traffic to Redwood during rollout.
[07:40] Sofia: operationally, how do we debug perf regressions? are there per-token traces?
[07:46] Derek: our console has token-level latency breakdowns, model-level tracing hooks, and error heatmaps. we can also provide tracing for canary runs.
[07:56] Liam: ok, agreed. last quick question: if we need to run on-prem completely air-gapped, is that doable?
[08:01] Derek: yes, we have an on-prem package; it's heavier to stand up and requires a bit more ops time but supported.
[08:10] Maya: great. to recap: Maya will send hosting/pricing comparison and a short pilot proposal; Derek will send security/compliance and integration tech notes; AtlasForge will confirm dataset and acceptance criteria; schedule technical deep dive next week. any other items?
[08:26] Oliver: nope, that's it from me.
[08:29] Liam: thanks everyone, good meeting.
[08:31] Maya: thank you, we'll follow up via email with attachments.

End of transcript.
